verdict.answer: Yes, but only as an exception. The normal daily limit is 9 hours of driving. You may extend it to at most 10 hours, but no more than twice in the same week (Monday 00.00 to Sunday 24.00). The 10-hour day still counts towards your other limits: no more than 56 hours of driving in the week and no more than 90 hours in any two consecutive weeks. Daily driving time is all driving between the end of one daily rest and the start of the next daily or weekly rest. There is also a separate emergency exception, for exceptional circumstances and only if road safety is not put at risk: you may exceed the daily limit by up to 1 hour to get to your employer's operational centre or your home for a weekly rest. This becomes up to 2 hours if you take an uninterrupted 30-minute break just before the extra driving and go home for a regular weekly rest. You must write the reason by hand on the record sheet, printout or duty roster, and make up the extra time with equivalent rest by the end of the third week after.

{"answerable":true,"answer":"Under Directive 2002/15/EC you count as a 'self-employed driver' only if you meet all of these conditions:
- Your main occupation is carrying passengers or goods by road for hire or reward, under a Community licence or another professional authorisation.
- You are entitled to work for yourself.
- You are not tied to an employer by an employment contract or any other working hierarchical relationship.
- You are free to organise your own working activities.
- Your income depends directly on the profits made.
- You are free to have commercial relations with several customers, on your own or through cooperation with other self-employed drivers.

A driver who does not meet these criteria has the same obligations and rights as an employed mobile worker under the Directive. The Directive has applied to self-employed drivers since 23 March 2009.","citations":[{"node_id":"2002/15:art3(e)","quote":""self-employed driver" shall mean anyone whose main occupation is to transport passengers or goods by road for hire or reward within the meaning of Community legislation under cover of a Community licence or any other professional authorisation to carry out the aforementioned transport, who is entitled to work for himself and who is not tied to an employer by an employment contract or by any other type of working hierarchical relationship, who is free to organise the relevant working activities, whose income depends directly on the profits made and who has the freedom to, individually or through a cooperation between self-employed drivers, have commercial relations with several customers."},{"node_id":"2002/15:art3(e)","quote":"those drivers who do not satisfy these criteria shall be subject to the same obligations and benefit from the same rights as those provided for mobile workers by this Directive"},{"node_id":"2002/15:art2(1)","quote":"this Directive shall apply to self-employed drivers from 23 March 2009"}]}

verdict.answer:
Under Directive 2002/15/EC you count as a 'self-employed driver' only if you meet all of these conditions:
- Your main occupation is carrying passengers or goods by road for hire or reward, under a Community licence or another professional authorisation.
- You are entitled to work for yourself.
- You are not tied to an employer by an employment contract or any other working hierarchical relationship.
- You are free to organise your own working activities.
- Your income depends directly on the profits made.

verdict.answer: When you travel with your vehicle by ferry or train, a regular weekly rest taken on board may be interrupted no more than twice by other activities (such as embarking or disembarking), lasting no more than one hour in total. For a regular weekly rest this is allowed only when both conditions are met: (a) the ferry or train journey is scheduled for 8 hours or more, and (b) you have access to a sleeper cabin on the ferry or train. Commission guidance note 6 (January 2017) says this derogation does not apply to any weekly rest. That note is older than the 2020 Mobility Package changes, so follow the current Regulation.

citations.quote: that period may be interrupted not more than twice by other activities not exceeding one hour in total
With regard to regular weekly rest periods, that derogation shall only apply to ferry or train journeys where:
the journey is scheduled for 8 hours or more; and
the driver has access to a sleeper cabin in the ferry or on the train.
The derogation under Article 9(1) does not apply to a weekly rest period, whether reduced or regular.

verdict.answer: Not yet, but they will. Today the EU driving time rules cover goods vehicles over 3,5 tonnes, so a 3-tonne van is outside them. From 1 July 2026 the rules also apply to international and cabotage goods transport in vehicles over 2,5 tonnes. The weight includes any trailer. From that date your cross-border 3-tonne vans will be covered. There is one exemption for vans between 2,5 and 3,5 tonnes. It applies only when the transport is not for hire or reward but on the own account of the company or driver, and driving is not the driver's main activity. If you deliver for customers for payment, or your staff are mainly drivers, the exemption does not help you.

verdict.answer: Yes. Since 2 February 2022 you must enter the symbol of the country you enter after crossing a border of a Member State. Do this at the start of your first stop in that country, and make that stop at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border. If you cross the border on a ferry or train, enter the country symbol at the port or station of arrival. You must also always enter the country symbols where your daily working period starts and finishes. You may take your driver card out to enter the country symbol after crossing a border. You don't have to enter the start and end country symbols if the tachograph records location data automatically under Article 8; the passage states this exemption only for those start and end entries.

citations.quote: From 2 February 2022 the driver shall also enter the symbol of the country that the driver enters after crossing a border of a Member State at the beginning of the driver’s first stop in that Member State.
That first stop shall be made at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border.
Where the crossing of the border of a Member State takes place on a ferry or train, the driver shall enter the symbol of the country at the port or station of arrival.
The driver shall enter in the digital tachograph the symbols of the countries in which the daily working period started and finished.
is necessary in order to enter the symbol of the country after having crossed a border
It shall not be necessary for drivers to enter the information referred to in the first subparagraph if the tachograph is automatically recording location data in accordance with Article 8.
